Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Start time: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Aaron Lee (Kestrel Head of ML), Maya Patel (Backend), Jordan Price (Security), Samir Gupta (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick sync on POC model selection, pinning strategy and fallback/rollback policies after this week's bench. Action items around sharing traces, pricing, and security artifacts. Customer leaning toward a dedicated pool if 99p latency meets target and cost delta is acceptable.

Topics:
- Bench results review (latency, quality)
- Model catalog comparison (open models vs optimized variants)
- Version pinning, rollbacks, and fallback routes
- Security/residency and data handling clarifications

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give a quick agenda — bench results, model choices, pinning strategy and then next steps. Miguel you want to start with performance summary?
[00:18] Miguel Santos: Yeah sure, um, I pulled the latest runs from the pilot cluster — this is the three-node dedicated-ish pool you guys spun up. We ran the traffic profile you sent us, about 40 rps bursty, median context length ~220 tokens, with a long tail to 1k tokens. The headline: Redwood-optimized model v1.4-q8_0 gives median token latency ~18ms/token, and p99 of generation latency for full 512-token outputs is around 820ms. There is some jitter during the long-tail sessions, which we traced to KV cache warmups and a couple of oversized batching events.
[00:52] Aaron Lee: Sorry, can you repeat the p99? 820ms for 512 tokens is the number?
[00:58] Miguel Santos: Yes, p99 end-to-end for a 512-token generation — about 820ms. For shorter prompts 128 tokens it's more like 230ms p99. We also tested a quantized variant v1.4-q4 which dropped p99 a bit but with slightly worse helpfulness scores on the eval set.
[01:18] Maya Patel: When you say 'helpfulness' how are you measuring that? Is it our rouge-like script or the human eval set we gave?
[01:26] Miguel Santos: Good question — it's the small human-annotated subset you shared plus an automated semantic-sim metric. So the q4 variant dropped ~3.5 points on our internal quality metric vs q8. That maps to some regression on entity extraction and sensitive phrase handling in a few cases.
[01:40] Jordan Price: That's the key for us — we can't accept regressions on PII redaction. Those are non-negotiable.
[01:45] Lena Park: Totally understood. That's why pinning and fallback are important — you can pin production traffic to v1.4-q8_0 and set a fallback to hosted v1.4-rt if the dedicated pool fails or misses SLOs.
[01:58] Samir Gupta: Quick clarification on 'hosted v1.4-rt' — that would be the Redwood managed endpoint?
[02:03] Lena Park: Yes, hosted, multi-tenant, same model family but routed through Redwood's hosted fleet with slightly higher latency but instant capacity.
[02:09] Aaron Lee: So how does graceful rollback work in practice? If we push pin to a model and something goes wrong, is traffic switched instant or gradual?
[02:17] Miguel Santos: You can configure rollouts — canary 10% for 30 minutes, then 50%, or instant cutoff. For emergency rollback, it's effectively instantaneous in the control plane: we change the routing policy and the router drains and shifts new sessions to the fallback. There will be some in-flight tokens on the old variant but no user-visible corruption; you can pair that with automatic alerting if 5xx rate or latency crosses thresholds.
[02:40] Maya Patel: Is there any chance of token duplication or session split when the KV cache is different across variants?
[02:47] Miguel Santos: Good catch — KV cache is per model variant and per GPU instance. Switching variants will create a cold cache for new sessions. For ongoing sessions, we keep the same serving host until the session ends; we don't migrate KV across architecture differences. We recommend short-lived sessions or warns in the app if you have long-lived stateful sessions.
[03:06] Aaron Lee: For our pipeline, most sessions are short, but a small percentage are multi-turn dialogues that need consistent context — not huge though.
[03:12] Jordan Price: Security side — how are logs and prompts handled in hosted vs dedicated? We need certs that prompts are not retained in the hosted layer beyond retention window and no customer PII is used for model training.
[03:24] Lena Park: On hosted, we have configurable retention and opt-out; for Dedicated and Private, data is isolated and Redwood does not use prompts for training. We can share SOC2, ISO27001 docs and specific language for contractual terms. I'll add those to next steps.
[03:36] Jordan Price: Please do. Also we need KMS integration details and whether keys are customer-managed in Dedicated.
[03:42] Miguel Santos: Dedicated supports customer-managed keys via KMS, and Private supports HSM in on-prem installs. We'll send the integration guide.
[03:50] Samir Gupta: Back to the bench numbers — can you share traces so our infra team can replay?
[03:55] Miguel Santos: Yes, I'll upload the raw traces and a small script to reproduce the 99p numbers. They include the request headers, payload sizes, and timing breakdowns. Note: traces have PII scrubbed, except for sample prompts you provided; we'll need the subset from Aaron to fully reproduce.
[04:12] Aaron Lee: I'll drop a sanitized set in the S3 link by Friday.
[04:16] Lena Park: For model selection, the team was comparing the Redwood-optimized family (v1.4 variants) vs the upstream open checkpoint (1.4-base) and Anthropic-esque similarity models. Miguel, what's the qualitative difference?
[04:30] Miguel Santos: On our eval sets, the optimized variants have better latency and similar or slightly better consistency due to attention kernel optimizations. The base open checkpoint is slightly better on rare factual recall for some prompts, but the delta is small. The trade is cost/throughput vs marginal quality differences. The q8_0 variant seems like the sweet spot for Kestrel given your throughput and quality requirements.
[04:53] Maya Patel: Can you remind us about cost difference between q8 and q4? ballpark numbers?
[04:58] Lena Park: Roughly q4 gives 20-30% lower compute costs but increases model variance; q8 is the middle ground. We'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet tonight — dedicated commit pricing also changes the math.
[05:08] Aaron Lee: Our main success criteria: p99 < 1s for 512 tokens, entity extraction F1 > 0.92, no PII leakage, and monthly cost under threshold X (Samir has that). If we meet that, we go to reserved capacity.
[05:22] Samir Gupta: Right, and timeline: if pilot looks good by 2 more weeks, we want to be ready to commit in early December.
[05:30] Miguel Santos: Sounds feasible. One more note on fallbacks — you can define per-route fallbacks; e.g., route 'sensitive-entities' to q8 only and fallback to hosted q8-rt, while general chat routes can use q4 with fallback to q8.
[05:46] Jordan Price: That per-route policy is helpful for us. We want the sensitive extraction to always hit the higher-quality variant even if cost is higher.
[05:54] Lena Park: We'll help set those routes in the pilot config. Also, in case of a model rollback, we can auto-enable a temporary throttling rule to protect the dedicated pool from bursts while you investigate.
[06:06] Aaron Lee: Any known issues with model pinning and A/B testing? We want to run canary for 10% traffic and compare entity F1 live.
[06:14] Miguel Santos: You can run canary and collect per-model metrics in Redwood Console; we expose token-level cost, latency, and custom eval hooks to push your entity F1 metrics. There's minor sampling noise but it's reliable for the 10% canary.
[06:28] Maya Patel: On the infrastructure side, are there connection limits per instance? We had a 40 rps burst earlier — how will dedicated scale?
[06:35] Miguel Santos: Dedicated autoscaling policies can be configured — you set headroom thresholds and we add GPU workers. For your workloads, I'd recommend target CPU/GPU headroom of 30% and burst buffer to handle 2x expected peak. We'll attach a recommended autoscale JSON.
[06:49] Aaron Lee: If we want to test a real rollback scenario, can you simulate a node outage so we can observe behavior?
[06:55] Miguel Santos: Yeah we can run a controlled failure in our staging replica of your dedicated pool and capture the routing switch. I'll coordinate with Lena to schedule that.
[07:03] Samir Gupta: Let's do that next Wednesday morning if possible.
[07:06] Lena Park: I'll propose times after the call.
[07:09] Jordan Price: Regarding retention and logs for audits: can you give us an export of the audit trail for the pilot period? We need to show who invoked models and what model versions.
[07:18] Lena Park: Yes, Redwood Console keeps per-request audit logs for Dedicated; we'll provide a limited export and can show the demo in the security deep dive.
[07:25] Aaron Lee: Quick question — we ran the open checkpoint on our infra in parallel last week. The quality was slightly different; were you using the identical tokenizer and byte-pair merges?
[07:34] Miguel Santos: There are small differences in tokenization and normalization across forks; we try to match the open upstream but our optimized runtime can have different handling for some control tokens. We can supply the exact tokenizer hashes and config.
[07:45] Maya Patel: That's important for reproducibility.
[07:48] Miguel Santos: Agreed.
[07:50] (brief cross-talk about scheduling)
[08:00] Lena Park: Okay wrapping up — recap: Miguel will upload traces + script, Lena will share pricing + config recommendations, Aaron will upload sanitized prompts, Jordan will schedule security deep dive. We'll schedule a controlled failure drill next week. Any final questions?
[08:18] Aaron Lee: No, thanks. This was helpful.
[08:21] Maya Patel: Thanks all.
[08:23] Lena Park: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
